blocks.text: 1. Epochs

blocks.alt: The full dataset seen once is one epoch, repeated many times

blocks.text: RMS Normalization, the final topic of the previous Normalization Techniques module, closed out that module's coverage of stabilizing activations. Epochs opens the Training Deep Networks module, shifting focus to the practical mechanics of training itself.

An epoch is one complete pass through the entire training dataset, a genuinely foundational unit of measurement covered in full depth throughout this topic, and a term used constantly throughout the rest of this module.
2. The Definition, In Full

This connects back to the training dataset, already covered throughout earlier modules. Every single training example gets used exactly once during a genuine epoch, with no example skipped and none repeated within that same pass.
That is genuinely one full epoch, the fundamental unit of training duration, and the term that virtually every training configuration and training curve throughout this module will reference.

blocks.text: 3. Training Almost Always Runs For Many Epochs

blocks.alt: One pass is not enough to learn well while many epochs learn properly

blocks.text: A genuinely important, real practical fact follows immediately. Training almost always runs for genuinely many epochs, not just one, since a single pass rarely gives the network enough exposure to learn well.

The network sees the same data repeatedly, refining its weights a little more each pass, gradually improving through the same Gradient Descent process already covered in the Backpropagation & Optimization module.
4. Epochs Versus Individual Weight Updates

blocks.alt: One epoch contains many weight updates inside it

blocks.text: This connects back to Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, already covered in the Backpropagation & Optimization module. One epoch typically contains many individual weight updates, not just one single update per epoch.
This holds since the dataset gets split into many mini-batches, covered further in the very next topic of this module, with one weight update happening after each individual mini-batch is processed.
5. The Risk Of Too Few Epochs

blocks.alt: Too few epochs lead to underfitting

blocks.text: This connects back to underfitting, already covered in its own dedicated topic. Too few epochs mean the network never gets enough exposure to the data to learn its underlying patterns well.

The weights simply have not had enough opportunity to converge toward a genuinely good solution, leaving the network stuck in a state that resembles the underfitting already covered in that earlier topic.
6. The Risk Of Too Many Epochs

blocks.alt: Too many epochs lead to overfitting

blocks.text: This connects back to overfitting, already covered in its own dedicated topic. Too many epochs mean the network keeps refining on the exact same training data long after it stopped genuinely improving on new data.
This produces the exact overfitting behavior already covered in that earlier topic, where training performance keeps climbing while genuine generalization performance quietly stalls or even declines.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: Neither too few nor too many epochs is a fixed number that applies universally. The right number of epochs, already covered throughout this topic, genuinely depends on the dataset, the network architecture, and the other hyperparameters in use.

blocks.text: 7. Monitoring Performance Across Epochs

blocks.alt: Each epoch gets validation checked and tracked over time

blocks.text: A genuinely important practice is to track validation performance after every single epoch, rather than only checking once training finishes, a direct, practical response to the risks already covered in the previous two sections.

This reveals whether more training genuinely still helps, or has started genuinely hurting, giving a genuinely clear, ongoing signal throughout the entire training process rather than only a final verdict.
8. The Connection To Early Stopping

This connects back to Early Stopping, already covered in the Regularization Techniques module. It works by stopping training once validation performance stops genuinely improving across epochs, exactly the monitoring already covered in the previous section.
This is a direct, practical application of the epoch-by-epoch monitoring already covered in this topic, turning that ongoing observation into a concrete, automated stopping decision.

blocks.text: 9. Reasoning About The Right Number Of Epochs

A genuinely small, simple dataset often needs fewer epochs before the network fully learns its available patterns, since there is genuinely less underlying structure left to extract from repeated passes.
A genuinely large, complex dataset often needs genuinely more epochs to see enough repeated exposure to converge well, since its richer underlying structure typically takes longer to fully learn.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely simple training loop structure, tracking loss across multiple epochs to illustrate the concept covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(100, 3))
true_weights = np.array([2.0, -1.0, 0.5])
y = X @ true_weights + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=100)

weights = np.zeros(3)  # starting weights, already covered in Weight Initialization
learning_rate = 0.05
num_epochs = 5  # already covered as the fundamental unit of training duration in this topic

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    predictions = X @ weights
    errors = predictions - y
    gradient = (2 / len(X)) * X.T @ errors  # already covered in Gradient Descent
    weights = weights - learning_rate * gradient
    loss = np.mean(errors ** 2)
    print(f"Epoch {epoch + 1}/{num_epochs}: loss={loss:.4f}, weights={np.round(weights, 3)}")

print("This entire loop of 5 epochs, already covered in this topic, made 5 full passes through the training dataset")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the loss steadily decreasing across epochs as the weights converge toward the true underlying values, exactly the gradual refinement already covered as the reason training runs for many epochs.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: An epoch is one complete pass through the entire training dataset.
Training almost always runs for many epochs, not just one, refining weights gradually.
One epoch typically contains many individual weight updates, one per mini-batch.
Too few epochs risks underfitting; too many epochs risks overfitting.
Monitoring validation performance after every epoch reveals whether more training still helps.
Early Stopping is a direct, practical application of this epoch-by-epoch monitoring.
Dataset size and complexity are key factors in reasoning about the right number of epochs.
